prompt: Consider the view that all thinking is a bodily process like perceiving, as the ancients held, and evaluate whether Aristotle's critique of this view depends on his theory of phantasia.

This materialist thesis rested upon the principle that like is known by like — that the soul, composed of the same elements as the world, grasps those elements through corporeal contact. Aristotle's critique of this position, however, depends crucially upon his capacity to distinguish φαντασία from αἴσθησις, thereby demonstrating that certain cognitive operations irreducible to perception exist and thus that thinking cannot be exhaustively described as a bodily process. (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. sight or seeing: imagination takes place in the absence of both, as e.g. in dreams" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43). This contrast is decisive; phantasia operates when the sensory organs are inactive, thereby establishing an interval between bodily reception and the soul's image-making capacity. Hawhee underscores phantasia's rhetorical significance by noting its connection to suasion and desire, observing that people "desire to see and possess many things after hearing about" them, which indicates that phantasia mediates between linguistic persuasion and appetitive movement in ways that exceed mere sensory contact (Hawhee 2011, p. [PAGE NEEDED]). Papachristou, for her part, insists that the Greek word "phantasia" resists simple translation as "imagination," preferring to leave the term untranslated in order to preserve its technical distinctiveness within Aristotle's psychology (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10). This terminological caution signals the complexity of phantasia's internal grades — from sensory phantasia, which operates close to perception, to deliberative phantasia, which involves calculative comparison of images — a distinction that will be developed more fully in subsequent sections. Thus Aristotle's critique of the ancients begins precisely at the point where phantasia's contrast with aisthesis reveals thinking to be something more than bodily reception. 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia: The Image as Medium of Thought If phantasia is not reducible to perception, its product — the φάντασμα, the sensory image — likewise cannot be understood as a mere physical trace. Aristotle makes clear that "to the thinking soul images serve as if they were contents of perception (and when it asserts or denies them to be good or bad it avoids or pursues them)" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 47–48). The phantasma thus occupies a double role: it is at once an object of contemplation in itself (a θεώρημα) and a likeness (εἰκών) of what it represents. This representational duality constitutes what we may identify as the central tension at the heart of Aristotle's philosophy of mind — how the soul recognizes a present image as standing for an absent thing without already possessing independent access to that absent thing. 6). Burke, accordingly, observes that imagination serves to "recommend the dictates of reason to imagination, in order to excite the appetite and will," drawing attention to the way phantasmata function not merely as passive residues but as active mediators between rational judgment and desiderative response (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 93–96). 

## 3. Phantasia and Mneme: Memory, Image, and the Perception of Time The relationship between phantasia and memory (μνήμη) further illuminates why Aristotle cannot accept the ancients' identification of thinking with bodily process. Memory, Aristotle insists, requires the perception of time: "All memory, therefore, implies a time elapsed; consequently only those animals which perceive time remember, and the organ whereby they perceive time is also that whereby they remember" (Aristotle, *On Memory*, p. 1). The faculty that perceives time is not a discrete sense-organ but rather the common sense operating through phantasia — the capacity to hold before the soul an image that is simultaneously grasped as past. This temporal dimension of the phantasma distinguishes memory from immediate perception; memory's object is not present to the senses but is re-presented through an image that the soul recognizes as a likeness of a prior experience. The representational puzzle thereby reappears: the phantasma must function both as an intrinsic object of contemplation and as a sign pointing beyond itself to an absent past. White's account of phantasia's structural position within *De Anima* helps to clarify this mediating role, for he situates phantasia among the "properties of which the essence is the cause," treating it as a power that enables higher cognitive operations including memory and anticipation (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 6). Burke, in a related vein, notes that imagination alters the will through its conjunction with "religion, opinion, and apprehension," suggesting that memory's phantasmata do not merely preserve the past but reshape the agent's dispositional orientation toward the future (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 93–96). The distinction between sensory and deliberative grades of phantasia is pertinent here as well: while sensory phantasia merely retains perceptual residues, deliberative phantasia actively compares and arranges images across temporal intervals, enabling the kind of practical reasoning that memory supports. The full implications of this distinction for Aristotle's account of belief will be addressed in the following section. 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa: Imagination, Belief, and the Limits of Bodily Explanation Aristotle's most trenchant argument against the materialist reduction of thinking to perceiving turns on the distinction between phantasia and δόξα (belief or opinion). The ancients' principle that like is known by like, as White reports, could not account for error, since error would consist in contact with the unlike — the very opposite of knowing by similarity (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23). Phantasia, by contrast, can be true or false independently of the agent's convictions; one may entertain a frightening image without thereby assenting to the belief that the object is genuinely threatening. Aristotle's example of the sun appearing a foot wide while one knows it to be larger than the earth illustrates this disjunction: the phantasma persists even when doxa contradicts it. Heidegger's reading of Aristotle's rhetorical psychology is instructive here, for rhetoric directs attention to κρίσις — "view-construction, a definite decision in the sense of a δόξα" — and that the speaker must bring the audience "into a corresponding frame of mind through discourse itself" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 124). phantasia is the faculty through which appearances are phenomenologically manifested — a dimension of sensory-imaginative presence not captured by the ancients' substance-based account of cognition. Indeed, Heidegger's broader concern with οὐσία as presence (Anwesenheit) intersects with phantasia's role as the mediating faculty of appearance: where the metaphysical tradition treats being as stable presence, phantasia introduces the dynamic, sometimes deceptive, manifestation of things to the soul. The voluntariness of phantasia — the fact that we can summon images before the mind's eye at will, as practitioners of mnemonic arts demonstrate — further separates it from doxa, which involves a commitment to truth that phantasia does not require (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43). Thus Aristotle's theory of phantasia does not merely supplement his critique of the materialist thesis; it is the very instrument by which that critique becomes possible, revealing irreducible dimensions of psychic life — temporal awareness, representational duality, the independence of image from belief — that no account of thinking as bodily process can adequately explain.
